title: Is there evidence for an association between changes in training load and running-related injuries? A systematic review
authors: Damsted C, Glad S, Nielsen RO, Sorensen H, Malisoux L
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
population: Runners aged 18-65 in randomized trials, prospective cohort, cross-sectional or case-control studies
findings: Only four articles met eligibility criteria; three found an association between increases in training load and higher RRI risk.
Recently changing velocity and/or distance and/or frequency was associated with injury versus non-injured runners (p = 0.037).
Increasing average weekly distance by more than 30% vs less than 10%: HR 1.59 (95% CI 0.96-2.66).
Total running distance in the week before injury origin was on average 86% higher than in other weeks (95% CI 12%-159%, p = 0.026).
No difference between a 10% and a 24% average increase in weekly volume (HR 0.8, 95% CI 0.6-1.3).
Authors conclude only very limited evidence supports a link between sudden load change and RRI (level of evidence 2).
limitations: Only four studies; heterogeneous exposures and populations; quality limited; predates Frandsen 2025. The 86% figure is a mean difference within injured runners, not a risk threshold.
implications: A 10% vs about 24% average weekly increase showed no injury difference, so a strict 10% weekly cap is not justified; use about 10% as default and allow more only with caution.
Do not derive a '1.5-2x weekly volume' flag from the 86% figure: it is a retrospective group mean, not a validated threshold.
Express weekly-progression messaging as soft guidance, never as a safety guarantee.

verification.notes: Crossref: IJSPT 13:931-942 (Dec 2018). Abstract matched. Added the p = 0.037 finding; removed the researcher's 1.5-2x flag implication as unsupported; grade lowered from A to B because the evidence base is four heterogeneous studies.
